title: What Caused the Civil War?
objective: After this level you can weigh the evidence on the war's causes, starting with what the seceding states said in their own declarations.
summary: Four seceding states explained themselves in declarations of causes, and Stephens called slavery the Confederacy’s cornerstone. Historians largely consider the Lost Cause false.

cards.headline: Why did the Deep South secede? The people who did it wrote down their answer.
cards.body: After the war, a very different answer spread. Weighing the two is a lesson in how to judge evidence.

cards.headline: Start with their own words
cards.body: Level 51 quoted Mississippi’s blunt line: “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery.” Mississippi wasn’t alone. Four seceding states, Texas, Mississippi, Georgia and South Carolina, issued declarations of causes explaining why they left the Union, and several named the defense of slavery as their reason. That’s primary evidence, written by the people making the decision, at the moment they made it.

cards.headline: The cornerstone
cards.body: Confederate leaders said the same thing in public. On March 21, 1861, Vice President Alexander Stephens gave what became known as the Cornerstone Speech. The new government’s cornerstone, he said, rested on slavery and on the claim that Black people were not equal to white people. This came from the top, at the start, out loud.

cards.headline: What about states’ rights?
cards.body: South Carolina’s declaration did talk about rights, so look at which ones. It complained that Northern states had passed laws that nullified the federal acts for returning people who escaped slavery, like Level 49’s Fugitive Slave Act, or made them useless. The grievance was that free states used their own powers to shield freedom seekers. As historians point out, the rights in question concerned slavery.

cards.headline: The Lost Cause
cards.body: After defeat, a new story took hold. Lost Cause writers claimed secession had little or nothing to do with slavery and was about states’ rights. Historians largely consider the Lost Cause beliefs false, because the evidence from the time of secession, the declarations and speeches above, says otherwise. On this question the evidence is settled.

mascot.line: Weigh sources by when they were made: the 1861 declarations outrank memories written after defeat.

cards.headline: What Caused the Civil War?: explained
learned: Four states explained secession in declarations of causes
Stephens: slavery was the Confederacy’s cornerstone
The “rights” South Carolina defended concerned slavery
Historians largely consider the Lost Cause false

questions.prompt: Match each source or story with what it said about secession.
questions.explanation: Alexander Stephens gave the Cornerstone Speech, Mississippi declared “Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery,” and Lost Cause writers later claimed secession was about states’ rights.

questions.prompt: A memoir written after the war says the South seceded only over states’ rights. Why do historians give more weight to the 1861 declarations?

options.label: They were written later, with more hindsight
options.rationale: The memoir is the later one; the declarations came first.

options.label: They were written by Northern critics of the South during the Civil War
options.rationale: The seceding states wrote them themselves.

options.label: They were written by the people deciding, at the moment they decided
They are shorter and easier to read
options.rationale: Length is no measure of reliability.

questions.explanation: The declarations are primary evidence from the decision-makers at the time; the Lost Cause was a later story that ignores them.

questions.prompt: South Carolina complained that Northern states blocked federal laws for returning freedom seekers. Which law did it want enforced?

options.label: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854
options.rationale: That act let settlers vote on slavery in the territories.

options.label: The Missouri Compromise
options.rationale: That drew a line for slavery in 1820.

options.label: The Indian Removal Act
options.rationale: That 1830 act pressed Native nations west.

questions.explanation: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required officials even in free states to arrest suspected freedom seekers; South Carolina protested that Northern states nullified such laws.
